diseases.name: Rabies
diseases.scientific_name: Rabies virus (genus Lyssavirus, family Rhabdoviridae) encephalomyelitis
diseases.urgency_criteria: Any bite, scratch or saliva contact from a dog, cat or other potentially rabid mammal is a time-critical exposure: wound washing and post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) assessment at an Animal Bite Treatment Center or emergency department are indicated the same day, because PEP is nearly 100% effective only when given before the virus reaches the central nervous system. Once neurological signs (hydrophobia, aerophobia, hypersalivation, agitation, paralysis) appear, rabies is almost universally fatal and the presentation is in the EMERGENCY tier for palliative and supportive care.
diseases.description: Rabies is an acute, progressive viral encephalomyelitis caused by rabies virus and related lyssaviruses, transmitted in the saliva of infected mammals through bites, scratches or contact with mucous membranes or broken skin. Dogs account for up to 99% of human cases worldwide, and about 40% of cases occur in children under 15. Once symptoms appear the disease is almost universally fatal, but it is preventable with prompt post-exposure prophylaxis. In the Philippines rabies causes the deaths of at least 200 Filipinos each year, and PEP is delivered through a network of government Animal Bite Treatment Centers under the National Rabies Prevention and Control Program.
diseases.pathophysiology: After inoculation the virus multiplies locally in muscle and enters peripheral nerves at the neuromuscular junction via nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. It travels centripetally by retrograde axoplasmic flow to the dorsal root ganglia and spinal cord and then to the brain, where replication increases exponentially in the setting of an inadequate interferon response. The virus then spreads centrifugally along nerves to peripheral tissues, including the salivary glands, where it is shed in saliva. Progressive inflammation of the brain and spinal cord produces the neurological syndrome and death.
diseases.clinicopathologic_correlation: Involvement of the dorsal root ganglion supplying the bite site explains early pain and paresthesia at a healed wound. Brainstem involvement produces violent pharyngeal muscle spasms triggered by attempts to swallow water or by air currents (hydrophobia, aerophobia). Viral spread to the salivary glands combined with inability to swallow produces hypersalivation and drooling. Limbic and cortical encephalitis produce anxiety, agitation, hallucinations and delirium, while autonomic involvement causes autonomic instability. In paralytic rabies, ascending flaccid paralysis begins in the exposed limb.
diseases.onset_progression: The incubation period is typically 2-3 months but ranges from about one week to one year. A prodrome of fever, malaise, myalgia, headache and pain, tingling or burning at the wound site is followed by the neurological phase. About 80% of patients develop furious (encephalitic) rabies with hyperactivity, agitation, hallucinations and hydrophobia; about 20% develop paralytic rabies with ascending paralysis starting in the exposed limb. Coma develops within about 10 days of neurological onset, and death typically follows within 2-3 days of coma, usually from cardiorespiratory arrest.
diseases.follow_up_monitoring: For exposed persons, the WHO exposure category is documented, the full vaccine schedule is completed on the scheduled days, and rabies immunoglobulin is given within 7 days of the first vaccine dose when indicated. Immunocompromised patients receive an additional vaccine dose. Previously vaccinated persons receive a shortened booster course without immunoglobulin. Patients with clinical rabies receive comprehensive palliative care, with sedation, analgesia, hydration and management of secretions.

causes: Infection with rabies virus or related lyssaviruses (family Rhabdoviridae), neurotropic RNA viruses
Transmission through saliva of an infected mammal by bites or scratches; dogs account for up to 99% of human cases
Contamination of mucous membranes or broken skin with saliva from an infected animal (for example, licks on broken skin)
Direct contact with bats (WHO category III exposure)
risk_factors: Bite or scratch from an unvaccinated or stray dog in a rabies-endemic area such as the Philippines
Childhood: about 40% of human rabies cases occur in children under 15 years
Delayed, incomplete or absent post-exposure prophylaxis after a category II or III exposure
Omission of rabies immunoglobulin after a category III exposure, or inadequate wound infiltration
Occupations with high exposure risk (veterinarians, animal handlers, laboratory staff) without pre-exposure prophylaxis
Residence in remote endemic areas with limited access to rabies biologicals
recommended_tests: Saliva RT-PCR for rabies virus RNA (part of the CDC antemortem specimen set)
Nuchal skin biopsy containing hair follicles, tested by direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) and RT-PCR
Cerebrospinal fluid for rabies virus neutralizing antibodies (RFFIT) and indirect fluorescent antibody testing
Serum rabies virus neutralizing antibodies (interpreted with vaccination history)
Postmortem confirmation by DFA or RT-PCR on brainstem and cerebellum tissue
Clinical classification of the exposure by WHO category (I, II or III); no test detects rabies infection before clinical onset
treatments: Wound management after exposure: thorough washing with soap and water for at least 15 minutes as soon as possible, followed by virucidal irrigation if available

Rabies vaccine for WHO category II and III exposures; CDC intramuscular schedule on days 0, 3, 7 and 14 (plus day 28 if immunocompromised); WHO dose-sparing intradermal regimens are used widely, including at Philippine Animal Bite Treatment Centers

Rabies immunoglobulin (human 20 IU/kg or equine 40 IU/kg) or rabies monoclonal antibodies for category III exposures (and for immunocompromised patients with category II exposures), infiltrated into and around the wound, given no later than 7 days after the first vaccine dose
Previously vaccinated persons: two vaccine doses (days 0 and 3) without rabies immunoglobulin, unless immunocompromised

Clinical rabies: no proven curative therapy; vaccine and immunoglobulin have no role once symptoms begin. Management is supportive and palliative (sedation for agitation, anticholinergics for secretions, opioid analgesia, intravenous fluids, antipyretics)
home_care: Immediate washing of any bite or scratch with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes, before travel to an Animal Bite Treatment Center
Same-day presentation to an Animal Bite Treatment Center or emergency department for PEP assessment after any animal bite or scratch
Completion of every scheduled vaccine dose on the assigned days, with the vaccination card kept for future exposures

prevention.content: Mass dog vaccination, including puppies, is the most cost-effective strategy for preventing human rabies because it stops transmission at its source (WHO). The DOH program targets elimination of human rabies by 2027 and a rabies-free Philippines by 2030.
Public education on dog behaviour and bite prevention, what to do after a bite or scratch, and responsible pet ownership.
Pre-exposure prophylaxis with rabies vaccine for people at high occupational risk and for those living in remote endemic areas with limited access to PEP.

Post-exposure prophylaxis by WHO category: category I (touching or feeding animals, licks on intact skin) needs wound washing only; category II (nibbling of uncovered skin, minor scratches or abrasions without bleeding) needs wound washing and immediate vaccination; category III (transdermal bites or scratches, saliva contact with mucous membranes or broken skin, direct bat contact) needs wound washing, vaccination and rabies immunoglobulin or monoclonal antibodies.

PEP delivered through government Animal Bite Treatment Centers run by the DOH and local government units under the Anti-Rabies Act of 2007 (RA 9482), with PhilHealth coverage for category II and III exposures.
Once symptoms emerge, WHO recommends comprehensive and compassionate palliative care, including sedation, analgesia, hydration and management of secretions.

emergency_signs: Any transdermal bite or scratch, or saliva contact with mucous membranes or broken skin, from a dog, cat, bat or other mammal
Pain, tingling or burning at a previous bite site, especially after a missed or incomplete PEP course
Painful throat spasms when trying to drink water or when air blows on the face (hydrophobia, aerophobia)
Excessive salivation and drooling with difficulty swallowing
Agitation, hallucinations, confusion or bizarre behaviour following an animal exposure
Progressive weakness or paralysis beginning in the bitten limb

differentials.distinguishing_feature: Trismus and generalized muscle rigidity with spasms and preserved consciousness; no hydrophobia or encephalopathy
Ascending symmetric weakness with areflexia and CSF albuminocytologic dissociation; mimics paralytic rabies but without bite-site paresthesia or progression to encephalitis

differentials.condition: Other viral encephalitis (e.g., Japanese encephalitis, herpes simplex encephalitis)
differentials.distinguishing_feature: No animal exposure history and no hydrophobia or aerophobia; different viral testing and imaging findings
No fever, hypersalivation, pharyngeal spasms or progressive neurological deficits

medicines.note: Core of PEP for WHO category II and III exposures and of pre-exposure prophylaxis; no role once clinical rabies has developed (StatPearls).

Indicated for category III exposures (and immunocompromised patients with category II); infiltrated into and around the wound within 7 days of the first vaccine dose. Not given to previously vaccinated persons.
Antipyretic and analgesic used in supportive and palliative care of clinical rabies (often rectal when swallowing is impaired).

diseases.name: Schistosomiasis (Schistosoma japonicum)
diseases.scientific_name: Schistosomiasis japonica (intestinal and hepatosplenic schistosomiasis due to Schistosoma japonicum)
diseases.urgency_criteria: Chronic abdominal pain, diarrhea or blood in the stool in a person with freshwater exposure in an endemic area warrants non-urgent clinical review with stool examination. Vomiting blood, black or bloody stools with dizziness (possible variceal bleeding from portal hypertension), rapidly increasing abdominal distension, or new seizures or focal neurological deficits place the presentation in the EMERGENCY tier.
diseases.description: Schistosomiasis japonica is a chronic parasitic disease caused by the blood fluke Schistosoma japonicum, acquired when larval cercariae released by infected freshwater snails penetrate the skin during contact with infested water. S. japonicum occurs in China, Indonesia and the Philippines, where 28 of 81 provinces are endemic, mainly in Eastern Visayas (Samar and Leyte), Mindanao and parts of Luzon such as Oriental Mindoro and Sorsogon. The DOH Schistosomiasis Control and Elimination Program estimates about 12.4 million Filipinos at risk. Disease results mainly from the host reaction to eggs, producing intestinal symptoms and, in advanced cases, liver fibrosis with portal hypertension. In Davao del Norte and Davao de Oro, surveys in 2024 found low prevalence (about 0.8% in school-aged children and 0.4% in adults), consistent with good morbidity control under mass drug administration rather than elimination.
diseases.pathophysiology: In endemic areas the snail Oncomelania hupensis quadrasi releases cercariae that penetrate human skin in freshwater. The larvae (schistosomula) migrate through the circulation, mature in the portal venous system and pair, and S. japonicum adults reside in the mesenteric veins, where females release eggs. Many eggs cross the intestinal wall and are passed in stool, but a large proportion are swept to the liver or remain trapped in tissues. Trapped eggs provoke granulomatous inflammation; in the liver this leads to periportal fibrosis and presinusoidal portal hypertension, with splenomegaly, collateral veins and ascites. S. japonicum is zoonotic, with carabao, cattle, dogs, pigs and rats among the many mammalian reservoir hosts that sustain transmission.
diseases.clinicopathologic_correlation: Egg-induced inflammation of the intestinal wall causes abdominal pain, diarrhea and blood in the stool. Periportal fibrosis with presinusoidal portal hypertension produces hepatosplenomegaly, ascites and portosystemic collaterals, which can bleed. Chronic blood loss and inflammation contribute to anemia, and in children to stunting and reduced learning ability. Acute schistosomiasis (Katayama syndrome), an immune reaction around the time of early egg laying, produces fever, rash, headache, myalgia, respiratory symptoms and eosinophilia. Ectopic egg deposition in the brain or spinal cord rarely causes granulomatous central nervous system lesions.
diseases.onset_progression: Acute schistosomiasis (Katayama syndrome) may appear about 14-84 days after exposure, usually in previously unexposed persons. Chronic infection develops over months to years with intermittent abdominal pain, diarrhea and blood in the stool. With heavy or prolonged infection, hepatosplenic disease with liver fibrosis, portal hypertension and ascites develops over years. Reinfection is common where water contact continues, so disease often reflects cumulative exposure.
diseases.follow_up_monitoring: Repeat stool examination about 1-2 months after praziquantel to confirm cure, with retreatment if eggs persist. Abdominal ultrasound assesses periportal fibrosis, hepatomegaly and splenomegaly in chronic disease. Patients with portal hypertension are followed for signs of variceal bleeding and ascites. In endemic communities, repeated treatment through mass drug administration is often required because of reinfection.
diseases.source_attribution: WHO fact sheet Schistosomiasis; CDC Clinical Overview of Schistosomiasis and Clinical Care of Schistosomiasis; Tabilin et al., Trop Med Infect Dis 2025 (Schistosomiasis in the Philippines); Belizario et al., Parasitol Int 2024 (Davao de Oro and Davao del Norte); DOH Philippines Schistosomiasis Control and Elimination Program; Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed.
causes: Infection with the trematode Schistosoma japonicum (blood fluke)
Skin penetration by cercariae released from infected Oncomelania hupensis quadrasi snails during contact with infested freshwater
Environmental contamination with eggs in human and animal feces, sustaining the snail-human cycle
Zoonotic reservoir hosts (carabao, cattle, dogs, pigs, rats) that maintain transmission
risk_factors: Residence in an endemic province in the Philippines (for example, Samar, Leyte, Oriental Mindoro, Sorsogon, and in Mindanao including Davao del Norte and Davao de Oro)
Routine agricultural, domestic, occupational or recreational contact with infested freshwater (rice fields, streams, irrigation canals)
School-aged children who swim or fish in infested water
Inadequate sanitation and hygiene, with open defecation near water sources
Close contact with infected animal reservoir hosts such as carabao near snail habitats
Missed rounds of mass drug administration in endemic communities
recommended_tests: Stool microscopy for S. japonicum eggs by the Kato-Katz technique (the primary diagnostic method used in the Philippines); multiple samples improve sensitivity
CBC with differential (eosinophilia, particularly in acute schistosomiasis; anemia in chronic disease)
Schistosome serology or circulating antigen detection when stool microscopy is negative but suspicion remains
Molecular testing (PCR) of stool or serum where available; more sensitive than Kato-Katz in light infections
Abdominal ultrasound for periportal fibrosis, hepatomegaly and splenomegaly
Repeat stool examination 1-2 months after treatment to confirm cure
treatments: Praziquantel is the treatment of choice; for S. japonicum the CDC regimen is 60 mg/kg per day orally in three divided doses for one day
In travelers, treatment is timed at least 6-8 weeks after the last freshwater exposure, when adult worms are mature and most susceptible
Repeat treatment after 2-4 weeks may be needed in lightly infected patients with persistent eggs
Praziquantel can be given to children from about 2 years of age, and WHO supports its use in pregnancy and lactation in mass drug administration settings
Management of complications of portal hypertension (variceal bleeding, ascites) follows standard hepatology and gastroenterology care
home_care: Completion of the full praziquantel dose on the treatment day, taken with food
Avoidance of wading, bathing, swimming or washing in streams, ponds and rice fields in endemic areas
Use of sanitary toilets so that feces do not reach water sources
Return for follow-up stool examination after treatment

prevention.content: Access to safe water, improved sanitation (toilets) and hygiene education to interrupt contamination of freshwater with eggs (WHO WASH strategy).
One Health snail control (habitat modification such as weed clearance, and molluscicides) together with management of infected animal reservoir hosts such as carabao.
Avoiding contact with infested freshwater in endemic areas, especially for school-aged children who swim or fish.

Large-scale preventive chemotherapy (mass drug administration) with praziquantel for preschool-aged children, school-aged children and at-risk adults in endemic areas, repeated yearly in high-transmission areas; in the Philippines, control under the DOH Schistosomiasis Control and Elimination Program has centered on preventive chemotherapy with praziquantel.
Stool surveillance (Kato-Katz) in endemic barangays to detect and treat infected persons before hepatosplenic disease develops.
Treatment reverses anemia, stunting and reduced learning ability in children; ultrasound follow-up and management of portal hypertension complications limit morbidity in advanced disease.

emergency_signs: Black, tarry or large-volume bloody stools, especially with dizziness or fainting
Rapidly increasing abdominal distension from ascites
Seizures, severe headache or new focal weakness (possible CNS egg deposition)
High fever with rash, cough and marked eosinophilia after recent freshwater exposure (acute schistosomiasis)

differentials.distinguishing_feature: Trophozoites or cysts rather than schistosome eggs on stool examination; liver abscess rather than periportal fibrosis

differentials.condition: Chronic hepatitis B or other causes of cirrhosis
differentials.distinguishing_feature: Hepatocellular dysfunction and cirrhotic nodular liver, with viral markers; schistosomal periportal fibrosis causes presinusoidal portal hypertension with relatively preserved liver function
May resemble acute schistosomiasis with fever and hepatosplenomegaly, but shows positive blood culture and lacks eosinophilia

differentials.condition: Colorectal neoplasia or inflammatory bowel disease
differentials.distinguishing_feature: Blood in stool without freshwater exposure or schistosome eggs; diagnosed by colonoscopy and biopsy

medicines.note: Drug of choice for all major Schistosoma species; S. japonicum 60 mg/kg/day in three divided doses for one day (CDC). Used in DOH mass drug administration.
Symptomatic relief of fever and pain (e.g., acute schistosomiasis); keep within maximum daily dose in patients with advanced liver disease.
NSAIDs increase gastrointestinal bleeding risk, a concern in hepatosplenic schistosomiasis with portal hypertension and varices; paracetamol is generally preferred.

diseases.name: Pertussis (Whooping Cough)
diseases.urgency_criteria: Coughing fits, an inspiratory whoop or vomiting after coughing, especially with a pertussis contact or incomplete vaccination, warrant prompt clinical review for testing and early antibiotics. Infants under 6 months, and any patient with apnea, cyanosis, severe hypoxia, respiratory distress, poor feeding, seizures or pneumonia, are in the EMERGENCY tier and usually require hospitalization.
diseases.description: Pertussis (whooping cough) is a highly contagious respiratory infection caused by the gram-negative coccobacillus Bordetella pertussis, spread by respiratory droplets with humans as the only reservoir. It is characterized by prolonged paroxysmal coughing with an inspiratory whoop and post-tussive vomiting. Young infants have the highest risk of severe disease, apnea and death. The Philippines experienced a pertussis surge in 2024: DOH data for January 1 to March 16, 2024 recorded 568 cases and 40 deaths, with 62.7% of cases in infants below six months and 67.6% of all cases unvaccinated or of unknown vaccination status.
diseases.pathophysiology: B. pertussis attaches to ciliated respiratory epithelium using adhesins such as filamentous hemagglutinin and pertactin. Tracheal cytotoxin damages ciliated cells and impairs mucociliary clearance, while pertussis toxin disrupts immune signaling and causes lymphocytosis. The organism remains on the respiratory mucosa rather than invading the bloodstream, and the toxin-mediated damage and impaired clearance produce the prolonged, paroxysmal cough. Marked leukocytosis is associated with pulmonary hypertension in severe infant disease.
diseases.clinicopathologic_correlation: Loss of ciliary clearance and airway irritation produce clusters of rapid coughs without time to inhale, followed by a forced inspiration against a narrowed glottis (the whoop) and often vomiting. Young infants may not generate a whoop and instead present with apnea and cyanosis. Pertussis toxin-driven lymphocytosis and hyperleukocytosis contribute to pulmonary hypertension. Forceful coughing can cause rib fractures, subconjunctival hemorrhage, syncope and urinary incontinence, and hypoxia can lead to seizures and encephalopathy.
diseases.onset_progression: The incubation period is about 7-10 days. The catarrhal stage (1-2 weeks) resembles a common cold with coryza, low-grade fever and a mild, occasional cough. The paroxysmal stage follows with numerous rapid coughs, the inspiratory whoop and post-tussive vomiting; paroxysms can reach about 15 per day, are more frequent at night and last about 2-3 weeks or longer. In the convalescent stage the cough subsides gradually over weeks, and paroxysms may recur with later respiratory infections. Adolescents and adults often have milder illness without a whoop.
diseases.follow_up_monitoring: Hospitalized infants are monitored for apnea, hypoxia and bradycardia, with attention to feeding, hydration and weight. White blood cell counts are followed in severe infant disease because extreme leukocytosis is associated with pulmonary hypertension. Close contacts are assessed for antibiotic post-exposure prophylaxis within 21 days of the index patient's cough onset, and vaccination status of the patient and household is reviewed and updated.
diseases.source_attribution: StatPearls: Pertussis (Vijayan, Daley; updated 2026); CDC Clinical Features of Pertussis and Treatment of Pertussis; PIDSP Childhood Immunization Schedule 2026; PIDS Research Paper 2022-04 (EPI assessment); Philippine News Agency report of DOH surveillance data (March 2024); Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics, 22nd ed.
causes: Infection with Bordetella pertussis, a gram-negative coccobacillus
Person-to-person spread by respiratory droplets from coughing or sneezing; humans are the only reservoir
Toxin-mediated damage to ciliated respiratory epithelium (pertussis toxin, tracheal cytotoxin)
risk_factors: Infancy, especially under 6 months of age and before completion of the primary vaccine series
Mother not vaccinated with Tdap during pregnancy
Household contact with an infected adolescent or adult, whose illness is often mild or unrecognized
Waning immunity years after childhood vaccination
Community outbreaks with low immunization coverage
recommended_tests: Nasopharyngeal swab or aspirate PCR for B. pertussis (first-line; most useful within about the first 4 weeks of cough)
Nasopharyngeal culture on specialized media (highly specific; results take 7-10 days)
Serology from about 3-12 weeks after cough onset; not used in infants under 6 months or recently vaccinated persons
CBC with differential for lymphocytosis and leukocytosis
Pulse oximetry and cardiorespiratory monitoring in infants
Chest radiograph when pneumonia is suspected
treatments: Azithromycin is the preferred antibiotic for all ages, including infants under 1 month despite a small association of macrolides with infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
Clarithromycin is an alternative macrolide; erythromycin is generally avoided in infants under 1 month
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is an alternative for macrolide intolerance or resistance in patients aged 2 months and older

Antibiotics are most effective in the first 1-2 weeks; treatment is recommended within 3 weeks of cough onset for persons aged 1 year and older and within 6 weeks for infants and pregnant women, mainly to reduce transmission
Treatment may start before test results when clinical suspicion is high or the patient is high risk or in contact with infants or pregnant women
Supportive care with hospitalization for infants under 6 months or those with apnea, hypoxia, pneumonia or pulmonary hypertension (oxygen, suctioning, hydration and nutrition support)
home_care: Completion of the full antibiotic course as prescribed
Small, frequent feeds or meals, especially after coughing fits with vomiting, with attention to fluid intake
Limiting close contact with infants and pregnant women while infectious, particularly before effective antibiotic therapy
Avoidance of smoke and other airway irritants that may trigger paroxysms

prevention.content: Routine infant vaccination with a DTP-containing vaccine (the pentavalent DPT-HepB-Hib vaccine of the Philippine Expanded Program on Immunization) as a 3-dose primary series at 6, 10 and 14 weeks, with DTP boosters at 12-18 months and 4-6 years and Tdap at 7-18 years (PIDSP 2026 schedule; PIDS 2022 EPI assessment).
Maternal Tdap vaccination at 27-36 weeks of gestation in each pregnancy, which reduces pertussis hospitalization in early infancy by more than 90% and deaths by about 95%.

Antibiotic post-exposure prophylaxis (same macrolide regimens as treatment) for household contacts and high-risk contacts such as infants, pregnant women and immunocompromised persons, ideally within 21 days of the index case's cough onset.
Early testing and antibiotic treatment of suspected cases, with droplet precautions, to limit spread to infants and other vulnerable contacts.
Hospital care for high-risk infants with monitoring for apnea and hypoxia and management of complications such as pneumonia, seizures and pulmonary hypertension.

emergency_signs: Pauses in breathing (apnea) in an infant
Bluish or gray color of the lips or face (cyanosis) during or after coughing fits
Difficulty breathing, fast breathing or low oxygen saturation
Poor feeding, dehydration or repeated vomiting in a young infant
Fever with worsening breathing suggesting pneumonia

differentials.condition: Viral respiratory infections (e.g., RSV bronchiolitis, adenovirus)
differentials.distinguishing_feature: Shorter course, often with fever and wheeze; lacks prolonged paroxysms with whoop and post-tussive vomiting
Prolonged cough in older children and adults with fever, headache and radiographic infiltrates; PCR distinguishes
Pertussis-like but usually milder illness without marked lymphocytosis; identified by species-specific PCR
Sudden onset of cough or choking without a catarrhal prodrome; focal findings on examination or imaging
Recurrent wheeze and variable airflow limitation responsive to bronchodilators; no whoop or post-tussive vomiting

medicines.note: Preferred antibiotic for treatment and post-exposure prophylaxis at all ages, including infants under 1 month (CDC, StatPearls).
Alternative macrolide; macrolides are used with caution in infants under 1 month because of the association with infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, where azithromycin is preferred.
Alternative for macrolide allergy, intolerance or resistance; not used in infants under 2 months.
